module_title: Microbiology and Biochemistry of Anaerobic Digestion

lessons.title: The Four Stages of Anaerobic Digestion: Hydrolysis, Acidogenesis, Acetogenesis, Methanogenesis
lessons.body: Anaerobic digestion happens in four sequential stages, each carried out by different groups of bacteria. Understanding these stages helps you diagnose problems when your digester underperforms. In hydrolysis, complex organic matter (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) is broken down into simpler soluble molecules like sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids. This is the slowest step for tough materials like crop residues or straw. For example, maize stover may take weeks to hydrolyse, while cow dung hydrolyses in days. In acidogenesis, fermentative bacteria convert these simple molecules into volatile fatty acids (VFAs), alcohols, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide. This stage is fast and can cause acid buildup if the next stage lags. In acetogenesis, syntrophic bacteria convert VFAs (like propionate and butyrate) into acetic acid, hydrogen, and CO2. This step is sensitive to hydrogen partial pressure; if hydrogen accumulates, acetogenesis stops. Finally, methanogenesis uses two main pathways: acetoclastic methanogens convert acetic acid to methane and CO2, while hydrogenotrophic methanogens combine hydrogen and CO2 to form methane. Methanogens are slow-growing and sensitive to pH, temperature, and toxins. In a typical African digester using cattle manure, the entire process takes 20â40 days. If hydrolysis is slow, you can pre-treat feedstock by chopping or soaking. If acidogenesis outpaces methanogenesis, you get acidification. Keep all four stages balanced by maintaining stable temperature (30â37Â°C for mesophilic), pH 6.8â7.4, and a consistent feed rate. Monitor VFA/alkalinity ratio weekly; if it exceeds 0.4, reduce feeding. Remember: the four stages are a chainâweak links break the whole system.

lessons.title: Key Microbial Groups: Fermentative Bacteria, Syntrophs, Methanogens
lessons.body: Three main groups of microorganisms drive anaerobic digestion: fermentative bacteria, syntrophs, and methanogens. Each has different roles, growth rates, and sensitivities. Fermentative bacteria are the workhorses. They break down sugars, amino acids, and fats into VFAs, alcohols, hydrogen, and CO2. They grow fastâdoubling in 30 minutes to a few hoursâand tolerate a wide pH range (5.0â8.0). In a digester fed with cassava peels, fermentative bacteria quickly produce acids, which can drop pH if not buffered. Syntrophs are a special group that work in pairs with methanogens. They convert propionate and butyrate into acetate, hydrogen, and formate. Syntrophs are slow growers (doubling in 2â6 days) and are inhibited by high hydrogen levels. They depend on methanogens to consume hydrogen and keep its partial pressure low. If methanogens are stressed (e.g., by ammonia or temperature shock), hydrogen builds up, syntrophs stop, and VFAs accumulate. Methanogens are archaea, not bacteria. They are the slowest growers (doubling in 3â10 days) and the most sensitive. Acetoclastic methanogens (e.g., Methanosarcina) convert acetate to methane; hydrogenotrophic methanogens (e.g., Methanobacterium) use hydrogen and CO2. Methanogens require pH 6.8â7.4, temperatures 30â37Â°C (mesophilic) or 50â55Â°C (thermophilic), and trace metals like nickel and cobalt. In African digesters, ammonia from poultry litter can inhibit methanogens at total ammonia nitrogen above 3,000 mg/L. To keep all groups healthy, feed consistently, avoid sudden temperature changes, and add trace element supplements if needed. A balanced community means stable biogas production.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Microbial Activity: Temperature, pH, Alkalinity
lessons.body: Three key factors control microbial activity in your digester: temperature, pH, and alkalinity. Get these right, and biogas production is steady. Temperature: Most African digesters run in the mesophilic range (30â37Â°C). Methanogens are very sensitive to fluctuationsâeven 2Â°C change can reduce biogas by 10â20%. In hot climates, digesters may overheat above 40Â°C, so shade them or use underground insulation. In cooler highlands, you may need a greenhouse or compost jacket to maintain 35Â°C. Never let temperature swing more than 1Â°C per day. pH: Optimal pH is 6.8â7.4. Below 6.6, acid-producing bacteria thrive while methanogens slow, causing acidification. Above 7.8, ammonia toxicity increases. Measure pH daily with a calibrated digital meter or pH strips. If pH drops, add lime or sodium bicarbonateâbut first check alkalinity. Alkalinity: This is the buffering capacity, mainly bicarbonate. It neutralises acids and keeps pH stable. For stable operation, alkalinity should be 2,000â5,000 mg/L as CaCO3. If alkalinity is below 1,000 mg/L, the digester is vulnerable to acid shock. You can raise alkalinity by adding agricultural lime (calcium carbonate) or wood ash. In a typical 6 mÂ³ fixed-dome digester in Kenya, adding 500 g of lime when pH drops to 6.7 can restore balance. Monitor the VFA/alkalinity ratio: if it exceeds 0.4, reduce feeding and add buffer. Remember, pH is a symptom; alkalinity is the cause. Test both weekly. Keep recordsâa simple notebook works. If you maintain temperature, pH, and alkalinity within range, your microbes will reward you with consistent methane.

lessons.title: Monitoring Microbial Health: VFA/Alkalinity Ratio, FOS/TAC
lessons.body: To keep your digester healthy, you need to monitor microbial activity before problems become visible. The two most practical tests are the VFA/alkalinity ratio and FOS/TAC. VFA/alkalinity ratio: This is the concentration of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) divided by total alkalinity, both measured in mg/L as CaCO3. A healthy digester has a ratio between 0.1 and 0.4. If it rises above 0.4, acid-producing bacteria are outpacing methanogensâearly warning of acidification. If it drops below 0.1, the digester may be underfed. You can measure VFAs with a simple titration kit (e.g., Hach or Hanna) or send samples to a lab. Alkalinity is measured by titrating with sulfuric acid to pH 4.3. For a small farm in Uganda, a weekly test using a $50 titration kit is enough. FOS/TAC: This is a German standard (FOS = volatile organic acids, TAC = total alkalinity). It is essentially the same as VFA/alkalinity but expressed as a ratio of acetic acid equivalent to CaCO3. Target FOS/TAC: 0.2â0.4 for stable operation. Above 0.5 indicates overloading; below 0.2 suggests underfeeding. Many African biogas programmes now use handheld FOS/TAC meters (e.g., from Bioprocess Control) that give results in 10 minutes. If you cannot afford a meter, use the simple titration method: add 0.1N sulfuric acid to 20 mL of digestate until pH 5.0, then continue to pH 4.3. The volume used between pH 5.0 and 4.3 correlates with VFAs. Record results weekly. If ratio is high, stop feeding for 2â3 days, mix the digester, and add lime or sodium bicarbonate. If ratio is low, increase feeding gradually. Consistent monitoring prevents crashes and keeps biogas flowing.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Microbial Issues: Acidification, Ammonia Inhibition
lessons.body: Two common microbial problems in African biogas digesters are acidification and ammonia inhibition. Learn to spot them early and act fast. Acidification: This happens when acid-producing bacteria grow faster than methanogens, causing VFAs to accumulate and pH to drop below 6.6. Symptoms: sharp drop in biogas production, sour smell, pH below 6.6, VFA/alkalinity ratio above 0.5. Causes: overfeeding (especially with sugary or starchy waste like fruit peels or molasses), sudden temperature drop, or lack of buffering. Fix: Stop feeding immediately. Mix the digester gently to distribute alkalinity. Add lime (calcium carbonate) or sodium bicarbonate: for a 6 mÂ³ digester, add 1â2 kg of lime dissolved in water. Check pH daily. Resume feeding only when pH is above 6.8 and VFA/alkalinity ratio is below 0.4. To prevent, feed consistently and avoid shock loads. Ammonia inhibition: This occurs when total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) exceeds 3,000â4,000 mg/L, especially from poultry litter, pig manure, or urine. Symptoms: biogas production drops, pH rises above 7.8, and you smell ammonia. Methanogens are inhibited, but acidogens may still produce VFAs. Fix: Dilute the digester contents with water (add 20â30% fresh water), stop feeding high-nitrogen feedstock, and add a carbon-rich material like maize stover or sawdust to adjust the C/N ratio. You can also add zeolite or clay minerals to adsorb ammonia. In severe cases, you may need to empty part of the digester and refill with fresh manure and water. Prevention: Balance your feedstockâmix poultry litter with cattle manure or crop residues to keep C/N ratio between 20 and 30. Monitor TAN monthly if using high-nitrogen waste. Keep records. Early action saves your digester.

lessons.title: Lab Exercise: Measuring Biogas Potential (BMP Test)
lessons.body: A Biochemical Methane Potential (BMP) test measures how much methane a feedstock can produce. It helps you choose the best mix for your digester. Here is a simple lab exercise you can do with basic equipment. Materials: 1 L glass bottles with airtight caps, rubber tubing, a water displacement setup (or a gas bag), a water bath or incubator set to 37Â°C, a pH meter, and a source of inoculum (digestate from a working digester). Feedstock: Dry and grind your sample (e.g., cow dung, maize stover, food waste). Procedure: 1. Prepare inoculum by incubating fresh digestate at 37Â°C for 3â5 days to degas. 2. In each 1 L bottle, add 200 mL inoculum and a known amount of feedstock (e.g., 5 g volatile solids). For a blank, use only inoculum. 3. Fill bottles with distilled water to 500 mL, flush with nitrogen gas to remove oxygen, and seal. 4. Incubate at 37Â°C for 30 days. 5. Measure biogas volume daily using water displacement (acidified water to prevent CO2 dissolution) or a gas bag. 6. Analyse methane content with a gas chromatograph or a simple CO2 scrubber (pass gas through NaOH solution; remaining volume is methane). 7. Calculate methane yield: mL CH4 per g volatile solids added. Typical values: cow dung 200â300 mL/g VS, maize stover 300â400 mL/g VS, food waste 400â500 mL/g VS. In Africa, you can adapt this using plastic bottles, syringes, and a thermometer. If you lack a gas chromatograph, use a portable biogas analyser (e.g., Geotech GA5000). Run tests in triplicate. Record results. Use BMP data to design your digester and choose feedstock mixes. For example, if your cow dung gives 250 mL/g VS and you feed 10 kg VS per day, you can expect about 2.5 mÂ³ of methane dailyâenough to cook for a family of six.

quiz.q: Which stage of anaerobic digestion breaks down complex organic matter into simple soluble molecules?
quiz.explanation: Hydrolysis is the first stage where enzymes break down carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids.

quiz.q: Which microbial group is the slowest growing and most sensitive to pH and temperature?
quiz.explanation: Methanogens are archaea that grow slowly and require strict pH 6.8â7.4 and stable temperatures.

quiz.q: What is the optimal pH range for anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: Methanogens function best at pH 6.8â7.4; outside this range, acidification or ammonia toxicity occurs.

quiz.q: Which test measures the ratio of volatile fatty acids to alkalinity?
quiz.explanation: FOS/TAC and VFA/alkalinity ratio are essentially the same test, expressing VFAs relative to buffering capacity.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of acidification in a digester?
options: B) Sharp drop in biogas production
quiz.explanation: Acidification causes VFA accumulation, pH drop below 6.6, and a sharp decrease in biogas production.

quiz.q: Which feedstock is most likely to cause ammonia inhibition?
quiz.explanation: Poultry litter has high nitrogen content, leading to ammonia levels that can inhibit methanogens.

quiz.q: What is the target VFA/alkalinity ratio for a healthy digester?
quiz.explanation: A ratio between 0.1 and 0.4 indicates stable operation; above 0.4 signals acidification risk.

quiz.q: Which microbial group converts propionate and butyrate into acetate, hydrogen, and formate?
quiz.explanation: Syntrophs work in partnership with methanogens to convert VFAs like propionate and butyrate.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for mesophilic anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: Mesophilic digesters operate best at 30â37Â°C, with minimal fluctuations.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a method to increase alkalinity in a digester?
options: A) Add lime or sodium bicarbonate
quiz.explanation: Lime (calcium carbonate) or sodium bicarbonate adds buffering capacity to neutralise acids.

quiz.q: In the BMP test, what does BMP stand for?
quiz.explanation: BMP stands for Biochemical Methane Potential, a measure of methane yield from a feedstock.

quiz.q: Which gas is produced by hydrogenotrophic methanogens?
quiz.explanation: Hydrogenotrophic methanogens combine hydrogen and CO2 to produce methane.

quiz.q: What is the typical methane yield from cow dung in a BMP test?
quiz.explanation: Cow dung typically yields 200â300 mL methane per gram volatile solids.

quiz.q: Which factor is most critical to monitor daily in a digester?
quiz.explanation: pH is a quick indicator of imbalance; daily measurement helps catch problems early.

quiz.q: What is the role of syntrophs in anaerobic digestion?
options: B) Convert VFAs to acetate and hydrogen
quiz.explanation: Syntrophs oxidise VFAs like propionate and butyrate into acetate, hydrogen, and formate.

quiz.q: Which condition can cause acidification in a digester?
quiz.explanation: Overfeeding with easily degradable sugars leads to rapid VFA production and pH drop.

quiz.q: What is the recommended C/N ratio for stable anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: A C/N ratio of 20â30 balances nitrogen for microbial growth and prevents ammonia inhibition.

quiz.q: Which tool can be used to measure biogas volume in a simple BMP test?
quiz.explanation: Water displacement is a low-cost method to measure gas volume by displacing acidified water.

quiz.q: What does a high VFA/alkalinity ratio indicate?
quiz.explanation: A ratio above 0.4 means VFAs are accumulating faster than they are consumed, risking acidification.

quiz.q: Which microbial group is inhibited by high hydrogen partial pressure?
quiz.explanation: Syntrophs require low hydrogen partial pressure to convert VFAs; high hydrogen stops their metabolism.

quiz.q: What is the first action when you detect acidification?
options: B) Stop feeding and add buffer
quiz.explanation: Stop feeding to reduce acid production, and add lime or bicarbonate to restore pH.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a symptom of ammonia inhibition?
options: B) pH above 7.8 and ammonia smell
quiz.explanation: Ammonia inhibition raises pH above 7.8 and produces a pungent ammonia odour.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding trace metals like nickel and cobalt to a digester?
quiz.explanation: Methanogens require trace metals such as nickel and cobalt for enzyme function.

quiz.q: In a BMP test, why is the inoculum incubated before use?
options: B) To degas and activate microbes
quiz.explanation: Incubating inoculum at 37Â°C for 3â5 days allows residual biogas to escape and microbes to become active.

quiz.q: Which stage of anaerobic digestion produces acetic acid, hydrogen, and CO2?
quiz.explanation: Acetogenesis converts VFAs like propionate and butyrate into acetic acid, hydrogen, and CO2.

quiz.q: What is the typical alkalinity range for stable anaerobic digestion?
quiz.explanation: Alkalinity of 2,000â5,000 mg/L as CaCO3 provides adequate buffering against acid shocks.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a practical way to prevent ammonia inhibition?
options: B) Mix high-nitrogen feedstock with carbon-rich material
quiz.explanation: Balancing feedstock with carbon-rich materials like maize stover keeps C/N ratio in the optimal range.

quiz.q: What does FOS/TAC measure?
options: B) Ratio of volatile organic acids to total alkalinity
quiz.explanation: FOS/TAC is the ratio of volatile organic acids (FOS) to total alkalinity (TAC), indicating digester stability.

quiz.q: Which microbial group produces methane from acetic acid?
quiz.explanation: Acetoclastic methanogens, such as Methanosarcina, convert acetate to methane and CO2.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if VFA/alkalinity ratio is below 0.1?
quiz.explanation: A ratio below 0.1 suggests underfeeding; slowly increase feedstock to boost microbial activity.
